results.title: GOP tax cuts pushed red state to the brink as auditor's warning came true: analysis
results.description: Nearly a decade ago, then-Auditor Nicole Galloway issued a stark warning. Her February 2018 budget stress test found Missouri increasingly dependent on individual income taxes and ill-equipped to weather an economic downturn. “If there are economic bumps in the road ahead,” she said, “our state is not prepared.” The report got a round of news stories. Then everyone moved on. Five months later, then-Gov. Mike Parson signed legislation touted as the largest single-year income tax cut in Missouri history. Flash forward to last week, when a task force studying Missouri’s public school funding formula was told the legislature will likely need to cut $1.5 billion to $3.5 billion from what state agencies want to spend next year. Missouri faces nearly $3 billion gap between spending requests and tax revenue So what happened between the warnings and public discussion of a multibillion-dollar budget hole? Federal pandemic assistance and unexpectedly strong tax collections helped Missouri build a massive surplus. By June 2023, the state’s general revenue fund held approximately $5.8 billion. That gave lawmakers room to invest, increase spending and cut taxes. So they did all three. In 2022, Parson signed another income tax cut he called the largest in state history, estimated to reduce annual revenue by $764 million. A year later, lawmakers eliminated state income taxes on Social Security and public pension payments, at an estimated cost of $309 million a year. Then, in 2025, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed legislation eliminating the state income tax on capital gains — profits from selling investments. Originally estimated to cost $111 million annually, the exemption proved considerably more expensive. Its impact on fiscal 2026 revenue was later estimated at more than $500 million. Meanwhile, spending grew. Galloway’s successor, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, documented just how quickly. From fiscal 2020 to 2025, general revenue grew 45.8%, while spending increased 53.4%. Inflation over that period was 24.5%. Not all that spending growth was discretionary. Medicaid costs increased, pandemic assistance expired and maintaining existing programs became more expensive. Nor is every appropriated dollar spent. Agencies leave money unused because of vacancies and project delays. Still, Missouri was authorizing more spending than it collected annually and relying on the surplus to cover the difference. Now the money that made those budgets possible is nearly gone. In December 2025, Fitzpatrick warned that continued deficit spending could exhaust the general revenue fund by fiscal year 2028. He repeated the warning in June, after lawmakers approved another budget exceeding projected revenue. Missouri auditor warns deep budget cuts loom as surplus nears end The Kehoe administration’s own budget instructions acknowledged that ongoing spending is projected to exceed recurring revenue by more than $1 billion. As The Independent’s Rudi Keller reported last week, agencies are requesting approximately $16.5 billion in general revenue next fiscal year — nearly $3 billion more than the state expects to collect in the current fiscal year. The governor’s budget office has projected that the once-enormous general revenue balance will shrink to $265 million by June 2027. And much of the pressure comes from costs lawmakers can’t easily avoid. Agency requests include more than $640 million in additional Medicaid expenses and $182 million for schools merely to maintain current funding. Hundreds of millions more in anticipated Medicaid and school costs aren’t included. Nearly two-thirds of general revenue operating spending goes to education, social services and mental health. Shield those departments, and finding $2 billion elsewhere becomes extraordinarily difficult. Further tax reductions remain on the agenda. Kehoe — who vetoed or froze nearly $500 million in the budget this year, arguing “we have a spending problem” — recently identified income and property tax policy among his economic development priorities, emphasizing helping Missourians keep more of their money. Meanwhile, incoming House Budget Chairman Bill Owen appears focused on the other side of the ledger. The Springfield Republican says his party has put its energy into cutting taxes without adequately scrutinizing spending. He plans to examine agency budgets line by line. That might uncover savings. But much of the budget, like Medicaid, is driven by enrollment and federal rules lawmakers don’t control. Lawmakers could also redirect money set aside for highways and Capitol renovations. That might provide temporary relief, but it wouldn’t fix the recurring imbalance. Which brings us back to Galloway. She worried about what a recession would do. Missouri got here without one. Years of tax cuts, increased spending and the depletion of a historic surplus have reshaped its finances. The state’s new revenue forecast arrives next month. Lawmakers return in January. The warnings have been on file for years. Missouri Independent is part of States Newsroom, a nonprofit news network supported by grants and a coalition of donors as a 501c(3) public charity.
